Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued 
by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. 
The increase is even more pronounced when China is excluded: debt stock owed 
to bondholders increased 11.1 percent, to $1.8 trillion, and debt stock owed to 
commercial banks and other private creditors rose 8.3 percent, to $2.3 trillion 
(figure 1.3). The increase in private lending, which is highly procyclical, was 
correlated with this group of countries’ robust economic growth, as measured by their 
gross national income (GNI), which grew 6.0 percent in 2025. Through the most 
recent crises, decreases in debt stock from this creditor base have been associated with 
the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 turbulence, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The 
robust 2025 economic growth of LMICs (excluding China) attracted lenders back 
to these economies, and many LMIC governments proved eager to borrow when 
international investors are willing to lend, even at elevated borrowing rates.
For this group of countries, the share of debt stock owed to bondholders by 
public sector entities stands at 82 percent, a much higher share than the PNG 
sector counterpart, and increased by 10.4 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. The 
opposite is true for debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private 
creditors, where an 83 percent share of the obligations is held by the PNG sector 
of the economy. This type of debt increased 7.0 percent to $1.9 trillion in 2025, 
and the debt stock of public sector entities owed to commercial banks and other 
private creditors saw a much larger increase of 15.1 percent, to $385.7 billion 
in 2025.

results.text:
[text_p034_b000 | World Bank International Debt Report 2026 | page 34 | TEXT]
INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
10
Japanese yen. The dollar’s dramatic 2025 depreciation inflates the size of external 
debt denominated in these currencies; that debt would appear to be more moderate 
if, for example, it was recorded in euros or other hard currencies.
The effect is particularly pronounced among the concessional arm of all 
multilateral creditors. SDR-denominated loans represent a significant share of 
outstanding concessional debt across multilateral institutions, and the dollar’s 
5.0 percent depreciation against the SDR in 2025 increased these loans’ dollar-
equivalent values correspondingly. Concessional repayment schedules further 
amplify the impact: because annual principal payments are small relative to 
outstanding balances, the dollar-equivalent currency revaluation of the debt stock 
tends to outweigh the modest stock reductions from debt servicing. For several 
of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 
2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some 
cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, 
leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing.
Of the $301.8 billion increase in LMICs’ PPG debt stock (external debt 
obligations of a country’s government and any private sector debts backed by a 
public sector guarantee) recorded in 2025, at least 28.2 percent can be attributed 
to the depreciation of the US dollar. Borrowing by the PPG sector of the economy 
gets reported at the instrument level and in the currency in which the liabilities 
are denominated or repaid. Accordingly, this level of detailed reporting makes 
possible the computation of the effect of the cross-currency valuation. 
Viewed from a lending category perspective, the external debt stock of countries 
eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing increased 
8.1 percent in 2025, to $1.3 trillion. Of this group, LICs’ debt increased at an 
even faster pace of 8.9 percent in 2025, to $262.4 billion, a marked increase not 
seen since 2020. Although LICs account for only a 2.8 percent share of total 
LMIC debt stock, over 60 percent of these countries are at high risk of debt 
distress or already in debt distress. An increase of such magnitude for this most 
vulnerable group of countries exacerbates their susceptibility to financial market 
volatility and stresses their already limited fiscal space. (Refer to box 1.3 for 
income and lending classifications.)
Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market 
conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of the borrower, 
saw a strong rebound in 2025. LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors 
increased 5.2 percent in 2025 to $5.0 trillion, compared to the 0.6 percent 
increase recorded in 2024. The increase in debt stock owed to private creditors 
was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and to commercial 
banks and other private creditors, which increased by 5.7 percent (to $2.4 
trillion) and 4.7 percent (to $2.7 trillion), respectively (figure 1.2).

[text_p027_b000 | World Bank International Debt Report 2026 | page 27 | TEXT]

1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks 
and Debt Flows as of End-2025
Trends in External Debt, 2015–25
Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased 
fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions 
of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external 
borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 
5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 
60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since 
the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was 
driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 
2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of 
US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced 
its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and 
the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), 
predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a 
rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new 
borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence 
after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small 
increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern 
shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in 
favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. 
(Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.)

Trends in External Debt of IDA-Eligible Countries, 2015–25
External debt stock of IDA-eligible countries reached a record $1.3 trillion in 
2025, accumulating at a rate of 8.1 percent, faster than that of the other LMICs. 
The pace of accumulation was much higher than the 2.9 percent average recorded 
during the past three years and raises sustainability concerns for this group of 
countries. Long-term debt stock rose by 7.9 percent, and short-term debt rose 
by 10.7 percent, bringing the end-2025 external debt stock to almost double the 
2015 level. Long-term obligations of the PPG sector grew at a faster rate of 9.0 
percent than the 4.3 percent increase of the PNG debt stock. As a share, PPG debt 
represented 76.3 percent of total long-term obligations of IDA-eligible countries, 
remaining almost unchanged from 2024 and 10 percent higher than in 2015. 
Debt stock owed to official creditors increased 8.1 percent to $722.1 billion in 
2025, representing 80.8 percent of long-term PPG debt. Obligations owed to this 
creditor group have remained stable over the past decade, but the composition 
has slightly changed over this period. In 2025, debt stock owed to official 
bilateral creditors increased 2.7 percent in 2025, to $241.5 billion, and debt 
stock owed to multilateral creditors also increased, by 11.0 percent to $480.6

After hitting an all-time high in 2024, the cost of servicing IDA-eligible countries’ 
external debt obligations (interest plus principal repayments) decreased 
2.3 percent in 2025, to $117.2 billion. The decrease in total debt servicing cost 
was due to a 2.9 percent decrease in principal repayments on total external debt, 
to $77.6 billion, which accounted for a 66 percent share of the total payments 
made by this group of countries in 2025. Interest payments on total liabilities 
also decreased, by 1.2 percent, to $39.6 billion in 2025, after recording a record 
high volume of $40.1 billion in 2024. From a debtor’s viewpoint, the decrease 
was led by PNG sector borrowing, which fell 9.5 percent to $40.9 billion, but 
the cost of servicing public sector debt continued to increase, by 2.5 percent, in 
2025 to $71.3 billion. Debt service payments on PPG debt have been on the rise 
for five consecutive years since 2020 and marked another record high for IDA-
eligible countries in 2025. The increase continues to limit these countries’ fiscal 
space and raises sustainability concerns for this group, which is eligible to borrow 
on concessional terms from IDA to support countries’ debt sustainability and 
includes some of the poorest countries.
Debt service payments from PPG borrowers to multilateral institutions and 
private creditors were the main drivers of the increase in total PPG debt service 
costs. Debt service payments to multilateral institutions increased 3.6 percent, to 
$30.6 billion, and accounted for 42.9 percent of PPG borrowers’ total payments. 
IDA-eligible countries owe more than half of their public sector debt to this group 
of creditors because of the concessional terms these institutions typically provide. 
Notably, as principal payments made to this creditor base increased 7.6 percent in 
2025, to $20.3 billion, interest payments decreased 3.5 percent to $10.3 billion. 
Debt service payments made by public sector entities to bondholders increased 
at a much faster pace of 16.9 percent, to $13.1 billion. Bondholders accounted 
for 18.4 percent of the debt service payments to PPG creditors, an increase of 
8 percentage points since 2023. This share has been increasing over the past two 
years, whereas the respective share in debt stock position has remained stable over 
the decade at an average of 12 percent. Principal repayments made to this creditor 
group increased 5.8 percent in 2025, to $6.6 billion, and included advance 
repayments from buyback operations made by Kenya and Suriname. Interest 
payments increased at a much faster pace of 30.7 percent in 2025, to $6.5 billion. 
These costs are projected to increase as IDA-eligible countries continue to tap 
international markets at an accelerated pace, amid an environment of elevated 
global interest rates.

2025, accumulating at a rate of 8.1 percent, faster than that of the other LMICs.

stock owed to multilateral creditors also increased, by 11.0 percent to $480.6

Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued 
by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. 
The increase is even more pronounced when China is excluded: debt stock owed 
to bondholders increased 11.1 percent, to $1.8 trillion, and debt stock owed to 
commercial banks and other private creditors rose 8.3 percent, to $2.3 trillion 
(figure 1.3). The increase in private lending, which is highly procyclical, was 
correlated with this group of countries’ robust economic growth, as measured by their 
gross national income (GNI), which grew 6.0 percent in 2025. Through the most 
recent crises, decreases in debt stock from this creditor base have been associated with 
the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 turbulence, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The 
robust 2025 economic growth of LMICs (excluding China) attracted lenders back 
to these economies, and many LMIC governments proved eager to borrow when 
international investors are willing to lend, even at elevated borrowing rates.
For this group of countries, the share of debt stock owed to bondholders by 
public sector entities stands at 82 percent, a much higher share than the PNG 
sector counterpart, and increased by 10.4 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. The 
opposite is true for debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private 
creditors, where an 83 percent share of the obligations is held by the PNG sector 
of the economy. This type of debt increased 7.0 percent to $1.9 trillion in 2025, 
and the debt stock of public sector entities owed to commercial banks and other 
private creditors saw a much larger increase of 15.1 percent, to $385.7 billion 
in 2025.

Elevated uncertainty matters because economies remain closely connected to 
international markets. Yet countries differ in the nature and degree of their 
external exposure, which shapes how global external shocks affect them. Trade 
provides an important example. As figure 2.2 shows, global imports and exports 
of goods and services increased from below 25 percent of gross domestic product 
(GDP) in the early 2000s, were halted by the 2008 global financial crisis, and 
subsequently rebounded and have fluctuated around 30 percent. Exposure,

of about 24 percent; trade flows were much more balanced in high-income

the roles of trade and financial exposure, exchange rates, inflation, and policy 
buffers, and how external debt can amplify vulnerabilities when shocks occur.

2. Debt Dynamics: Policy 
Implications
External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs
Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global 
uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, 
debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, 
and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This 
combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb 
when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to 
respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks 
alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens. Adverse 
developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter 
global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal 
positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development 
consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses.
International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens 
and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025). 
Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions 
between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify 
vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the 
channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter 
further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and 
changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt 
and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience. 
Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these 
interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a 
decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress.
Global uncertainty rose sharply in 2025 (figure 2.1) and remained elevated into 
2026. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more 
than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, 
nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index 
showed a similar pattern, rising sharply in early 2025 and remaining elevated into 
2026 (Ahir et al. 2022; Davis 2016).1

question: In Box 1.4 (page 38), what is the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) mechanism established by the G-7 for Ukraine?
answer: The Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) mechanism established by the G-7 for Ukraine is a distinct lending initiative where G-7 members committed approximately $50 billion in support to Ukraine, agreed upon in October 2024. This initiative is part of the broader financial support provided to Ukraine during the ongoing conflict, which includes various forms of assistance such as direct lending, grants, and guarantees [diagram_p038].

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
14
LMICs’ debt stock owed to all other creditor groups also increased in 2025. Debt 
stock owed to official creditors (public institutions such as national governments 
and international organizations) increased 8.4 percent in 2025, to $2.0 trillion. 
Lending by official bilateral creditors (national governments and their agencies) 
also showed a comeback, increasing 4.7 percent in 2025 after a 3.4 percent 
retrenchment in 2024. Support from multilateral institutions such as the World 
Bank Group and the IMF continued to be positive in 2025, but at a decreasing 
pace when compared to the COVID-19 pandemic era. Except for the multilateral 
support to Ukraine provided under the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration 
Loans for Ukraine initiative, the cumulative countercyclical lending by these 
institutions decelerated in 2025. (Box 1.4 describes the international support for 
Ukraine through this initiative.) LMICs’ debt stock owed to multilateral creditors 
increased 9.6 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. However, when the European 
Union’s support to Ukraine is excluded, debt stock owed to multilateral creditors 
increased 7.0 percent to $1.4 trillion in 2026. 
Box 1.4 International Support for Ukraine: The G-7 Extraordinary Revenue 
Acceleration
A Surge in Lending, Concentrated Among Official Creditors
Financial support for Ukraine from bilateral and multilateral creditors has reached 
unprecedented levels since the start of the Ukraine War in February 2022. Official 
creditors, including the Group of Seven (G-7) bilateral creditors and multilaterals 
like the European Union and the World Bank Group, provided $122.2 billion in 
disbursements during the 2022–25 period. This support reshaped the composition 
of Ukraine’s external debt (figure B1.4.1). Long-term external debt stock rose from 
$99 billion in 2015 to $227 billion in 2025, but little of that increase was driven by 
private creditors, whose claims remained broadly flat over the past decade, rising 
slightly from $72 billion to $82 billion. Debt owed to multilateral creditors accounts 
for most of the increase. Bilateral claims increased sixfold over the past decade but 
grew from a much smaller base and remained a modest share of the total. These 
official creditors delivered support to Ukraine not only through direct lending but 
also through grants, trust funds, guarantees, and co- and parallel financing, among 
other financial instruments.
The ERA and the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism
One such distinct lending mechanism is the G-7 Extraordinary Revenue

Financial support for Ukraine from bilateral and multilateral creditors has reached 
unprecedented levels since the start of the Ukraine War in February 2022. Official 
creditors, including the Group of Seven (G-7) bilateral creditors and multilaterals 
like the European Union and the World Bank Group, provided $122.2 billion in 
disbursements during the 2022–25 period. This support reshaped the composition

Box 2.3 External Shocks and Fiscal Consolidation
Fiscal consolidation following a major external shock is particularly difficult and 
less likely to preserve growth. For example, consolidation episodes preceded by 
terms-of-trade shocks were significantly less successful in maintaining per capita 
growth rates near preconsolidation rates than episodes that were not preceded 
by such a shock (figure B2.3.1). This result reflects not only policy choices but 
also the persistent economic damage caused by the shock and the need for 
governments to support vulnerable households and economic activity before 
adjustment can begin.
Consolidation is often delayed even after fiscal balances become unsustainable, 
which carries compounding costs. Where the primary deficit was significantly 
larger than what would stabilize debt, countries tended to wait three to four years 
before embarking on meaningful fiscal consolidation (figure B2.3.2; Di Lorenzo 
and Lacey 2024). Political and social constraints are particularly binding in the 
aftermath of a shock, but delay can compound the eventual costs. Where large 
sustainability gaps (that is, the primary deficit was significantly larger than what 
would stabilize debt) persisted for four years or more, the median debt ratio 
increased by 17 percentage points of gross domestic product. Growth also 
weakened: during periods of sustained fiscal unsustainability, average real gross 
domestic product per capita growth fell to the 32nd percentile of each country’s 
own historical distribution. For countries facing high borrowing costs and limited 
market access, these findings underscore the value of early, credible, and 
growth-conscious corrective action.
During commodity price booms and the resulting rise in fiscal revenues, 
governments in those economies tend to increase spending. Without primary 
surpluses, those economies tend to have fewer fiscal resources to support 
activity and protect vulnerable populations when external shocks hit. 
Increased spending and debt accumulation during booms may also lead 
to a loss of market confidence during commodity price busts, requiring a 
large fiscal adjustment or contributing to debt distress (refer to box 2.3 for 
more details on external shocks and fiscal consolidation). The implication 
is clear: fiscal strategies that save windfalls during economic upturns, such 
as commodity booms, and deploy those savings during downturns allow 
governments to respond effectively when shocks arrive.
(Box continues on next page)

The energy supply shock in 2026 has caused exchange rates in commodity-
importing LMICs to fall, worsening trade balances. Among commodity-importing 
LMICs with flexible or adjustable exchange rate regimes, currencies depreciated 
by about 1.7 percent between January and July 2026 (figure 2.5), on average. 
In contrast, currencies in commodity-exporting LMICs with flexible regimes 
appreciated by an average of 2.5 percent over the same period. Currency 
pressures have made imports more expensive in commodity importers and 
worsened trade balances. Across commodity-importing LMICs with flexible 
or adjustable currency regimes, merchandise import values, in US dollar terms, 
increased by an average 23 percent between February and June 2026 compared 
with the same months of 2025. Excluding China, the rate of increase was 
21 percent, on average. As import values increased faster than those of exports, 
merchandise trade deficits—without China—expanded in the first half of 2026. 
Between February and June 2026, merchandise trade deficits averaged almost 
$20 billion higher than in the same months of the previous year.

Elevated uncertainty matters because economies remain closely connected to 
international markets. Yet countries differ in the nature and degree of their 
external exposure, which shapes how global external shocks affect them. Trade 
provides an important example. As figure 2.2 shows, global imports and exports 
of goods and services increased from below 25 percent of gross domestic product 
(GDP) in the early 2000s, were halted by the 2008 global financial crisis, and

the roles of trade and financial exposure, exchange rates, inflation, and policy 
buffers, and how external debt can amplify vulnerabilities when shocks occur.

Transmission of External Shocks
External shocks are transmitted to LMICs differently, depending on their 
structural features. Economies that rely heavily on imports of goods and 
services for domestic activity are vulnerable to sudden changes in the external 
environment, such as production shortfalls in major supplier countries, export 
restrictions, or supply chain disruptions; in contrast, export-oriented economies 
are more vulnerable to shifts in demand among their trading partners. External 
shocks also tend to spill more forcefully into LMICs with open financial markets, 
partly reflecting rapid capital flow movements. In addition, the types of policy 
frameworks in LMICs are important for the transmission of external shocks. For 
example, in economies with flexible exchange rate regimes, the effects of external 
shocks are partly absorbed through currency movements. In economies with fixed 
exchange rate regimes, pressure on the exchange rate can be cushioned by using 
foreign reserves. As discussed later in this chapter, damage from external shocks 
that LMICs can absorb and the speed of subsequent recovery are also subject 
to the availability of fiscal buffers and the implementation of fiscal and foreign 
exchange policy frameworks.

Transmission of External Shocks
External shocks are transmitted to LMICs differently, depending on their 
structural features. Economies that rely heavily on imports of goods and 
services for domestic activity are vulnerable to sudden changes in the external 
environment, such as production shortfalls in major supplier countries, export 
restrictions, or supply chain disruptions; in contrast, export-oriented economies 
are more vulnerable to shifts in demand among their trading partners. External 
shocks also tend to spill more forcefully into LMICs with open financial markets, 
partly reflecting rapid capital flow movements. In addition, the types of policy 
frameworks in LMICs are important for the transmission of external shocks. For 
example, in economies with flexible exchange rate regimes, the effects of external 
shocks are partly absorbed through currency movements. In economies with fixed 
exchange rate regimes, pressure on the exchange rate can be cushioned by using 
foreign reserves. As discussed later in this chapter, damage from external shocks 
that LMICs can absorb and the speed of subsequent recovery are also subject 
to the availability of fiscal buffers and the implementation of fiscal and foreign 
exchange policy frameworks.

question: According to Figure 1.1 on page 30, what was the general trajectory of LMIC external debt stocks between 2015 and 2025?
answer: According to Figure 1.1 on page 30, the general trajectory of LMIC external debt stocks between 2015 and 2025 shows an increase, with a notable rise in debt accumulation returning to levels seen in 2019-20. This indicates a rebound in private investor confidence and lending, alongside continued support from multilateral creditors. By 2025, the total external debt for LMICs reached a record $9.2 trillion, marking the fastest increase since 2021, despite a decrease in China's external debt during the same period [chart_p030].

results.text:
[text_p027_b000 | World Bank International Debt Report 2026 | page 27 | TEXT]
3
1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks 
and Debt Flows as of End-2025
Trends in External Debt, 2015–25
Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased 
fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions 
of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external 
borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 
5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 
60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since 
the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was 
driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 
2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of 
US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced 
its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and 
the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), 
predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a 
rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new 
borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence 
after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small 
increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern 
shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in 
favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. 
(Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.)

Increased borrowing from private creditors has affected country lending groups 
disproportionately and has led to a hardening of the average terms of new loan 
commitments to IDA-eligible countries. These countries continued to face ever-
increasing average interest rates on their new commitments, with rates reaching 
8.2 percent in 2025, up 0.6 percentage point (figure 1.10). Such high average 
rates have not been seen since 1989 for this group of countries and pose a 
challenge for their economic development. By contrast, IBRD borrowers have 
seen improvements in their average terms of new commitments, with average 
interest rates decreasing from 5.8 percent in 2024 to 5.5 percent in 2025.
As IDA-eligible countries continued to tap international markets to issue new 
bonds, they needed to pay even higher interest rates to attract investors to these 
instruments. Average interest rates on external commitments of IDA-eligible countries 
to bondholders increased 1.0 percentage point in 2025 to 9.4 percent, and remained 
above rates of IBRD borrowers, which experienced a decrease of 0.3 percentage 
point to 5.5 percent (figure 1.11). The return of international investors to IDA-
eligible countries remains uneven, concentrated in the largest borrowers, and costly, 
as international investors have increased their search for yield. IDA borrowers have 
therefore absorbed global financial shocks disproportionately. The recovery of IDA-
eligible countries’ issuance at yields above 8 percent implies materially higher rollover 
costs and could place further pressure on interest-to-revenue ratios and financing 
needs. For many frontier issuers, the binding constraint has consequently shifted from 
market access to market affordability.

Although large LMICs received the bulk of personal remittances, the direct 
investment they received has stagnated. FDI can support productive capacity, 
employment, and technology transfer, whereas remittances primarily provide 
income directly to households and can help stabilize consumption and 
foreign exchange receipts. The rise in remittances has therefore provided an 
increasingly important external resource for LMICs, but it does not substitute 
for the longer-term productive investment associated with FDI.
Excluding China, one of the largest recipients of FDI in the world until 2022, 
LMICs saw their FDI grow by only 5.3 percent from 2011 to 2025, when 
investment to LMICs slowed. LMICs in Latin America and the Caribbean 
received most of the FDI in 2025, $134.2 billion, recovering from the sharp 
downturn caused by the COVID-19 pandemic: the region’s FDI decreased 
by $52.7 billion from $124.6 billion in 2019 to just $71.9 billion in 2020. 
Data show that FDI seems to concentrate in larger and more economically 
dynamic LMICs, making Brazil, India, Indonesia, Mexico, and Viet Nam some 
of the largest recipients of FDI. Together, FDI inflows to these five countries 
accounted for 52.7 percent of total FDI received by all LMICs in 2025, 
excluding China. Brazil alone received $62.4 billion in investment in 2025. 
IDA-eligible countries received only 20.1 percent of total FDI received by 
LMICs in 2025, at $67.1 billion.

question: In Figure 2.12 on page 90, how did the share of sovereign assets held by domestic banks evolve in IDA countries compared to IBRD countries?
answer: In IDA countries, domestic banks have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets compared to banks in IBRD countries. This trend reflects the less developed and less diversified private sectors in IDA countries, as well as fewer investment options compared to IBRD markets. The increase in sovereign exposure in IDA countries extends beyond the domestic banking sector to include the central bank and the domestic nonbanking sector [chart_p090].

Domestic creditors in both IDA and International Bank for Reconstruction and 
Development (IBRD) countries have elevated their exposure to the sovereign 
over the past 20 years. This move mirrors their respective governments’ growing 
reliance on domestic financing. However, domestic banks in IDA countries have 
consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than 
banks in IBRD countries have (figure 2.11). This higher exposure reflects less 
developed and less diversified private sectors in many IDA countries, as well as 
fewer investment options as compared to IBRD markets. Domestic banks may 
therefore have few alternatives to government securities, particularly during 
periods of financial stress. In IDA countries, the increase in sovereign exposure 
goes beyond the domestic banking sector to include the central bank and the 
domestic nonbanking sector (figure 2.12).
Consequently, domestic debt amortization dominates GFNs for LICs, signaling 
mounting liquidity pressures even where sovereign solvency appears contained. 
These pressures reflect the short average maturity of domestic debt in most LICs 
and the attendant rollover burden, whereby a growing share of gross financing 
serves merely to refinance maturing domestic obligations. To a lesser extent,

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
72
in healthy diet unaffordability over time, a broader outcome that reflects both 
food costs and people’s economic resources.
Food Import Shares in Poorer Economies
Across the sample, which consists predominantly of LMICs, the share of food in 
merchandise imports generally declines as income per capita rises (figure 2.13, 
panel a). By contrast, economies with larger external debt burdens relative to 
exports also tend to have higher food import shares (figure 2.13, panel b).5
Both relationships matter for an economy’s capacity to manage food import 
exposure. Lower-income economies may have less room to absorb increases in 
import costs, and a high debt-to-exports ratio indicates that external debt is 
large relative to export earnings. During external shocks, higher import costs can 
therefore coincide with weaker economic and external buffers; export earnings 
may also decline, further increasing pressure on foreign exchange resources and 
raising the debt-to-exports ratio, even without an increase in the debt stock.
Import Reliance and Debt Burdens Across Food Groups
Aggregate food import shares do not show how strongly the domestic supply of 
individual food groups depends on international markets. Net import reliance—
net imports as a share of domestic supply quantity—varies substantially across 
the six food groups making up the Healthy Diet Basket (Bai, Herforth et al. 2025; 
Herforth et al. 2025). Among net importing economies, median reliance is highest 
for oils and fats, at 63.6 percent, followed by starchy staples, at 36.9 percent, and 
legumes, nuts, and seeds, at 34.1 percent. Median reliance is lower for animal-
source foods, at 28.0 percent, and for vegetables and fruits, at 17.4 percent and 
13.4 percent, respectively.
To identify economies where high reliance on food imports and elevated 
external debt burdens overlap, figure 2.13 applies two reference thresholds. For 
many economies, high import reliance coincides with elevated external debt 
burdens. Figure 2.14 highlights economies where external debt stocks are at 
least 150 percent of exports, as a reference point based on the threshold applied 
under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative,6 and where net 
imports account for at least 30 percent of domestic supply in a given food 
group. The figure intends to identify the coexistence of these two sources of 
vulnerability, rather than to assess whether higher external debt is associated 
with greater reliance on food imports. This overlap is most common for oils and 
fats: 34 economies—about 42 percent of net importers in the group—meet both 
thresholds. The corresponding shares are about 28 percent for legumes, nuts, 
and seeds; 27 percent for starchy staples; 23 percent for animal-source foods; 
16 percent for vegetables; and 15 percent for fruits.

question: How did the 2026 Middle East conflict energy price shock (page 80) and food import dependency (page 96) combine to threaten external balances in low-income commodity-importing countries?
answer: The 2026 Middle East conflict caused a significant energy price shock, leading to increased inflation in commodity-importing low-income countries, which rose from 2.6% to 3.6% by June 2026. This inflation was exacerbated by rising energy prices and worsened trade balances due to currency depreciation, which averaged 1.7% among these countries. Consequently, merchandise import values surged by 23% compared to the previous year, resulting in expanded trade deficits averaging almost $20 billion higher than in the same months of 2025. This combination of rising inflation and deteriorating external balances posed a serious threat to the economic stability of low-income commodity-importing countries [chart_p080][chart_p081].

Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major

The energy supply shock in 2026 has caused exchange rates in commodity-

In contrast, currencies in commodity-exporting LMICs with flexible regimes

worsened trade balances. Across commodity-importing LMICs with flexible

merchandise trade deficits—without China—expanded in the first half of 2026.

$20 billion higher than in the same months of the previous year.

results.text:
[text_p079_b000 | World Bank International Debt Report 2026 | page 79 | TEXT]
2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs
55
2015–19 and 2020–25. Financial openness, represented by the sum of foreign 
assets and liabilities as a share of GDP, remained nearly unchanged from 
the mid-2010s through 2024. International financial integration has slowed 
since the pandemic in 2020, but that slowdown has been driven primarily 
by major economies; financial openness increased in almost 70 percent of 
LMICs between 2015–19 and 2020–24. In addition, as presented in chapter 1, 
external debt stocks in LMICs rose to $9.4 trillion by the end of 2025, an 
increase of $3.5 trillion since 2015.
The nature of external shocks also affects the different degrees of shock 
transmission to LMICs. For example, global supply shocks, including shortages 
of energy, food, and other commodities—and rapid increases in their prices, 
which tend to be caused by wars and conflicts as well as extreme weather-
related events—have a larger impact on commodity importers. The outbreak 
of a conflict involving major commodity producers can halt their exports, and 
the impact can be exacerbated by logistical disruptions such as port or shipping 
lane closures. Particularly in food-producing economies, disasters associated 
with extreme weather, including storms and droughts potentially caused by 
El Niño, can decrease global food production and disrupt global trade. In 
addition, abrupt shifts in trade policies, including the imposition of tariffs or 
export bans, can restrict access to key commodities. In contrast, commodity 
exporters tend to be affected more by adverse global demand shocks, including 
slowdowns in global activity triggered by major systemic events such as 
financial crises and pandemic-driven lockdowns, and the resulting plunges in 
commodity prices.
In commodity-importing LMICs, external shocks can be transmitted 
through multiple channels. Higher global energy and food prices, along 
with disruptions to shipping and global value chains, raise production 
and transportation costs. The resulting rise in domestic inflation in these 
economies drives up the cost of living, with disproportionate effects on 
poorer economies and households, where food accounts for a larger share of 
consumption. The purchasing power of consumers declines as real incomes 
fall, resulting in reduced spending. In addition, higher prices of commodities 
and other imported materials increase overall import costs, worsening terms 
of trade and current account balances. Financial conditions can tighten 
because of hikes in interest rates to combat increased inflation, raising 
borrowing costs. Pressures of currency depreciation rise, increasing the 
costs of servicing debt denominated in foreign currencies. Fiscal positions 
deteriorate, with increasing spending pressures, including fuel and food 
subsidies, and slower activity can lower revenue collection.

question: Relate the rising gross financing needs (GFNs) of IDA countries described on page 86 to the domestic debt service revenue burden shown in Figure 2.8 on page 85.
answer: The rising gross financing needs (GFNs) of IDA countries are closely linked to the increasing burden of domestic debt service. As domestic debt service-to-revenues ratio more than trebled, reaching almost 30 percent by 2025, this significant increase has reduced the resources available for public investment and other policy priorities. Consequently, a larger share of government revenues must be allocated to interest payments, which exacerbates the need for refinancing maturing obligations and contributes to the sustained increase in GFNs in IDA countries [chart_p085].

and the implementation of a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework to 
govern domestic debt issuance, including clear delineation of the roles of the

options for riskier external financing arrangements, sound debt management of

The World Bank Group tracks progress in borrowing countries’ public debt 
dissemination practices on an annual basis. Its assessment of these outcomes 
is presented in a heat map that measures the strengths and weaknesses of the 
dissemination practices in 76 IDA-eligible countries across nine key indicators: 
data accessibility, instrument coverage, sectoral coverage, information on recently 
contracted external loans, periodicity, time lag, debt management strategy, annual 
borrowing plan, and additional statistics and memo items.2
The Debt Reporting Heat Map shows that, over the past five years, IDA-eligible 
borrowers have made significant progress in public debt disclosure practices. 
In 2020, only 36 IDA-eligible countries, 47 percent of the 76 countries covered 
by the heat map, published fully accessible public debt data. The 2025 heat 
map found that 54 countries, or 72 percent, had fully accessible public debt 
data, a 25-percentage-point gain from 2020 (figure 3.1). Data accessibility in 
Sub-Saharan African countries has also improved significantly, rising from 
19 countries (50 percent of countries in the region) that published fully accessible 
data in 2020, to 29 countries (or 76 percent) in 2025 despite a regression 
in accessibility of data in some countries. These countries include Ethiopia, 
where data accessibility had deteriorated since it defaulted on its international 
bond in 2023, and Senegal, following the revelation by the auditors of a large 
understatement in the official debt statistics. Even in countries that have accessible 
data, important information gaps persist. Instrument coverage has improved, 
with 45 countries assessed as having full coverage in 2025 compared to 33 
countries in 2020, but progress has been slower than accessibility. Additionally, 
comprehensive sector coverage is limited, with subnational borrowing, contingent 
liabilities, and the obligations of SOE debt often excluded from the official public 
debt figure. Moreover, only about one-quarter of countries report instrument-
level information on the terms of newly contracted debt.

question: According to the overview on page 75, what is the core reason why external shocks can be more difficult to absorb when governments face substantial debt burdens?
answer: The core reason why external shocks can be more difficult to absorb when governments face substantial debt burdens is that these governments already have significant financing needs and limited room to respond. This situation makes them more vulnerable to adverse developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter global financing conditions, which can weaken their external and fiscal positions. High debt levels can amplify the economic and development consequences of these shocks and impair the effectiveness of policy responses [text_p075_b000].

results.title: Report Content Page 75 Part 0
results.text:
[text_p075_b000 | World Bank International Debt Report 2026 | page 75 | TEXT]
51
2. Debt Dynamics: Policy 
Implications
External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs
Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global 
uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, 
debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, 
and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This 
combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb 
when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to 
respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks 
alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens. Adverse 
developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter 
global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal 
positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development 
consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses.
International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens 
and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025). 
Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions 
between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify 
vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the 
channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter 
further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and 
changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt 
and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience. 
Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these 
interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a 
decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress.
Global uncertainty rose sharply in 2025 (figure 2.1) and remained elevated into 
2026. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more 
than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, 
nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index

Implications
External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs
Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global 
uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, 
debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, 
and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This 
combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb 
when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to 
respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks 
alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens. Adverse 
developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter 
global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal 
positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development 
consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses.
International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens 
and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025). 
Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions 
between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify 
vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the 
channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter 
further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and 
changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt 
and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience. 
Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these 
interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a 
decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress.

2026. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more 
than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, 
nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index 
showed a similar pattern, rising sharply in early 2025 and remaining elevated into 
2026 (Ahir et al. 2022; Davis 2016).1

question: Why does external debt denominated in foreign currencies increase macroeconomic vulnerability during global shocks as detailed on page 78?
answer: External debt denominated in foreign currencies increases macroeconomic vulnerability during global shocks because it amplifies the transmission of these shocks. 2015–19 and 2020–25. Financial openness, represented by the sum of foreign 
assets and liabilities as a share of GDP, remained nearly unchanged from 
the mid-2010s through 2024. International financial integration has slowed 
since the pandemic in 2020, but that slowdown has been driven primarily 
by major economies; financial openness increased in almost 70 percent of 
LMICs between 2015–19 and 2020–24. In addition, as presented in chapter 1, 
external debt stocks in LMICs rose to $9.4 trillion by the end of 2025, an 
increase of $3.5 trillion since 2015.
The nature of external shocks also affects the different degrees of shock 
transmission to LMICs. For example, global supply shocks, including shortages 
of energy, food, and other commodities—and rapid increases in their prices, 
which tend to be caused by wars and conflicts as well as extreme weather-
related events—have a larger impact on commodity importers. The outbreak 
of a conflict involving major commodity producers can halt their exports, and 
the impact can be exacerbated by logistical disruptions such as port or shipping 
lane closures. Particularly in food-producing economies, disasters associated 
with extreme weather, including storms and droughts potentially caused by 
El Niño, can decrease global food production and disrupt global trade. In 
addition, abrupt shifts in trade policies, including the imposition of tariffs or 
export bans, can restrict access to key commodities. In contrast, commodity 
exporters tend to be affected more by adverse global demand shocks, including 
slowdowns in global activity triggered by major systemic events such as 
financial crises and pandemic-driven lockdowns, and the resulting plunges in 
commodity prices.
In commodity-importing LMICs, external shocks can be transmitted 
through multiple channels. Higher global energy and food prices, along 
with disruptions to shipping and global value chains, raise production 
and transportation costs. The resulting rise in domestic inflation in these 
economies drives up the cost of living, with disproportionate effects on 
poorer economies and households, where food accounts for a larger share of 
consumption. The purchasing power of consumers declines as real incomes 
fall, resulting in reduced spending. In addition, higher prices of commodities 
and other imported materials increase overall import costs, worsening terms 
of trade and current account balances. Financial conditions can tighten 
because of hikes in interest rates to combat increased inflation, raising 
borrowing costs. Pressures of currency depreciation rise, increasing the 
costs of servicing debt denominated in foreign currencies. Fiscal positions 
deteriorate, with increasing spending pressures, including fuel and food 
subsidies, and slower activity can lower revenue collection.

68
borrowing increases exposure to exchange rate and refinancing shocks. At the 
same time, high debt limits countries’ ability to borrow to close financing gaps. 
Countries are therefore left increasingly exposed to shocks, with minimal fiscal 
and financial buffers.
Sound fiscal and debt policies are central to preparing for, responding to, and 
recovering from external shocks. Fiscal buffers and debt sustainability determine 
the extent to which countries can absorb shocks and support recovery. Countries 
that entered shock episodes with adequate fiscal buffers, manageable debt 
levels, and a track record of countercyclical policies consistently limited long-
term output losses. By contrast, high debt and procyclical spending amplified 
the economic damage.4 The interaction of limited fiscal buffers, elevated debt 
vulnerabilities, and weak policy execution points to three interconnected 
priorities: revenue mobilization and maintaining sound debt management, 
adopting countercyclical fiscal strategies, and investing in fiscal institutions.
Mobilizing revenue and managing debt. Revenue mobilization is not simply a 
matter of raising tax rates. Effective mobilization requires a holistic approach that 
strengthens the policy, administrative, and legal foundations of the tax system in 
tandem (Benitez et al. 2023). Without this broader institutional underpinning, 
additional revenue efforts risk being partial, inequitable, or unsustainable, 
undermining the fiscal resilience they are intended to build.
Effective debt management requires not only controlling the overall level of debt 
but also managing its composition and risk profile, including maturity, currency, 
interest rate, refinancing, and creditor risks. Sound debt management acts as a 
key shock absorber during times of crisis. Poor borrowing choices made during 
periods of stress can worsen liquidity and solvency risks, particularly when 
governments turn to short-term solutions that are less transparent or less market 
based, such as private placements or collateralized borrowing. These instruments 
may provide immediate financing, but they can also increase rollover risks, 
reduce transparency, constrain future policy choices, and expose public assets or 
future revenues to claims. Governments should therefore design, implement, and 
communicate contingent borrowing plans before crises occur.
Conducting fiscal policy over the economic cycle. Economies that ran 
procyclical spending policies and persistent deficits over time faced 
economically larger and longer-lasting output losses from external 
shocks, whereas those that maintained countercyclical spending and ran 
primary surpluses, on average, experienced little to no losses. Dependence 
on commodities for exports and fiscal revenues makes commodity-
exporting LMICs particularly exposed to swings in commodity prices.

The Growing Use of TRSs in Sovereign Financing
Since 2024, TRS arrangements have been identified in Angola, Argentina, 
Colombia, Nigeria, and Senegal, with financing amounts ranging from about 
$1.0 billion to $9.3 billion. Maturities have generally ranged from one to three 
years, and disclosed collateralization ratios have typically been between 133 and 
198 percent. Collateral has included domestic government securities, external 
sovereign bonds, US Treasury securities, or combinations of these instruments.
The transactions vary considerably in scale and collateral structure. In Argentina, 
the central bank entered a $3 billion, three-year TRS in 2025 backed by domestic 
government securities, although the collateralization ratio has not been publicly 
disclosed. Angola entered a $1.2 billion, one-year transaction in 2024 collateralized 
at 198 percent, equivalent to about $2.4 billion in collateral, primarily external 
sovereign bonds. In 2025, this financing was extended and increased to $1.5 billion 
for three years, with collateralization reduced to 148 percent, or approximately 
$2.2 billion. Angola also entered a separate $1 billion, three-year transaction 
in 2025 collateralized at 140 percent, using a combination of US Treasuries and 
domestic government securities.
Larger transactions demonstrate the potential scale of this financing. In Colombia, 
TRS transactions totaling approximately $9.3 billion in 2025 had a one-year 
maturity and collateralization of about 160 percent, implying approximately 
$15.1 billion in pledged external and domestic government securities. Nigeria’s 
$5 billion transaction in 2026 has a three-year maturity and collateralization 
of approximately 133 percent, corresponding to about $6.7 billion in domestic 
securities. In Senegal, seven TRS transactions contracted in 2025 provided 
approximately $1.1 billion in financing with three-year maturities and average 
collateralization of about 135 percent, corresponding to approximately $1.5 billion in 
pledged domestic government securities.

The recent transactions point to three common features:
• Large financing amounts: Transactions range from about $1.0 billion to 
$9.3 billion.

operation extended debt maturities and eased near-term refinancing pressures

debt stock.

$293.89 million of the 2028 notes and €411.66 million of the 2032 notes. These 
active liability-management measures helped stabilize the government’s debt 
indicators by smoothing out medium-term debt service.

results.title: Report Content Page 277 Part 0
results.text:
[text_p277_b000 | World Bank International Debt Report 2026 | page 277 | TEXT]
GLOssARy
253
Public debt is an external obligation of a public debtor, including all levels of 
government, the central bank, state-owned enterprises, public corporations, 
development banks, and any other autonomous public bodies of government.
Public domestic debt comprises debt liabilities owed by public sector entities to 
other resident units of the same economy.
SDR allocations are reserve-related liabilities, distributed to member countries in 
proportion to their quota shares at the International Monetary Fund. The SDR 
(special drawing right) allocations are included in the gross external debt position 
and classified as long-term special drawing rights.
Short-term external debt has an original maturity of one year or less. Available 
data permit no distinctions among public, publicly guaranteed, and private 
nonguaranteed short-term external debt.
State-owned enterprise is a corporate entity recognized by law that is at least 
partially owned by the government.
Total Return Swap is a financial derivative contract under which one party 
transfers the total economic return of a reference asset to another party in 
exchange for a predetermined stream of payments. The total return typically 
includes both periodic income generated by the asset, such as interest or coupon 
payments, and any capital gains or losses resulting from changes in the market 
value of the asset over the life of the contract. 
Treasury bonds are long-term debt securities with a maturity period of 20 or 
30 years. They are considered low-risk and are generally free of risk when held 
until maturity.
Variable-rate loans are loans for which the interest fluctuates according to 
changes in market interest rates.

The Growing Use of TRSs in Sovereign Financing
Since 2024, TRS arrangements have been identified in Angola, Argentina, 
Colombia, Nigeria, and Senegal, with financing amounts ranging from about 
$1.0 billion to $9.3 billion. Maturities have generally ranged from one to three 
years, and disclosed collateralization ratios have typically been between 133 and 
198 percent. Collateral has included domestic government securities, external 
sovereign bonds, US Treasury securities, or combinations of these instruments.
The transactions vary considerably in scale and collateral structure. In Argentina, 
the central bank entered a $3 billion, three-year TRS in 2025 backed by domestic 
government securities, although the collateralization ratio has not been publicly 
disclosed. Angola entered a $1.2 billion, one-year transaction in 2024 collateralized 
at 198 percent, equivalent to about $2.4 billion in collateral, primarily external 
sovereign bonds. In 2025, this financing was extended and increased to $1.5 billion 
for three years, with collateralization reduced to 148 percent, or approximately 
$2.2 billion. Angola also entered a separate $1 billion, three-year transaction 
in 2025 collateralized at 140 percent, using a combination of US Treasuries and 
domestic government securities.
Larger transactions demonstrate the potential scale of this financing. In Colombia, 
TRS transactions totaling approximately $9.3 billion in 2025 had a one-year 
maturity and collateralization of about 160 percent, implying approximately 
$15.1 billion in pledged external and domestic government securities. Nigeria’s 
$5 billion transaction in 2026 has a three-year maturity and collateralization 
of approximately 133 percent, corresponding to about $6.7 billion in domestic 
securities. In Senegal, seven TRS transactions contracted in 2025 provided 
approximately $1.1 billion in financing with three-year maturities and average 
collateralization of about 135 percent, corresponding to approximately $1.5 billion in 
pledged domestic government securities.
Common Features of Sovereign TRS Financing
The recent transactions point to three common features:
• Large financing amounts: Transactions range from about $1.0 billion to

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
40
2025, increasing 10.5 percent to $3.2 trillion, the pandemic era financing 
patterns reversed, recording an increase in inflows from private creditors and a 
simultaneous decrease in inflows from official creditors.
The increase in net debt flows from private creditors occurred because of 
a combined increase in net debt flows from bondholders and from banks 
and other private creditors. Net debt flows from bondholders increased 
73.6 percent in 2025, to $13.5 billion, and were mostly concentrated in 
borrowing by the public sector, which increased 57.4 percent to $11.9 billion. 
Net debt inflows from banks and other private creditors more than tripled to 
$10.4 billion in 2025. The increase was led by net flows to PNG borrowers, 
which account for a bigger share of the total and switched from an outflow 
of $572.1 million in 2024 to an inflow of $8.3 billion in 2025. Conversely, 
net flows from public sector borrowers to this creditor group decreased 
36.5 percent to $2.1 billion.
The restoration of access to capital markets has been particularly consequential 
for Sub-Saharan Africa, which accounted for 64 percent of IDA-eligible 
countries’ total public sector issuances (figure 1.19). The public sectors 
of eight countries in Sub-Saharan Africa collectively raised approximately 
$11.8 billion by end-December 2025, a marked 36.2 percent increase over 
2024. Several issuers returned after prolonged absences: Kenya, the largest 
issuer in the region, raised $3.5 billion in 2025. The country returned to bond 
markets to prepay its 2027 and 2028 maturity obligations ahead of schedule. 
Côte d’Ivoire raised a total of $2.5 billion in 2025. Importantly, a substantial 
share of proceeds from the two countries’ debt offerings funded their liability 
management operations, refinancing upcoming bullet maturities, and thereby 
easing rollover pressures. Nigeria, the third-largest issuer in the region, raised 
$2.3 billion in a dual-tranche international bond issue that was divided into 
one tranche with a 10-year maturity at 8.625 percent and a second, 20-year 
maturity tranche at 9.125 percent. Remarkably, Uganda’s share of domestic 
currency government debt held by nonresidents reached $2.8 billion in 2025, 
indicating strong demand for high-yield debt from international investors. 
Among countries in other regions, Uzbekistan recorded the highest international 
bond issuance among IDA-eligible countries in 2025, at $3.9 billion. The public 
sector issuance was divided between $1.6 billion in issuances from the general 
government sector, including issuances in domestic currency, and $2.4 billion 
in issuances from other public sector entities. Suriname completed its first 
international issuance since 2016.
